name: Livestock Improvement Corporation Limited
overview: LIC is a New Zealand farmer-owned co-operative that supplies bovine genetics (artificial breeding straws, including sexed semen), herd testing/DNA genomics, and MINDA farm-management software to New Zealand's roughly 10,000 dairy herds, with a smaller international genetics export business (Australia, Ireland, UK and other markets). Its core proprietary asset is a genetic database built over 100 years of NZ pasture-based dairy breeding, now underpinned by more than two million genomic profiles. FY2026 (year ended 31 May 2026) revenue was NZ$314.8m, statutory NPAT NZ$21.3m and underlying earnings NZ$21.8m, with the co-operative debt-free and holding NZ$60.3m cash.

business_model.summary: LIC sells genetics and services to farmer-shareholders and non-shareholder dairy farmers, priced under co-operative principles (fair commercial return, not profit maximisation). Revenue is a mix of highly seasonal, point-in-time product/insemination-service sales (NZ market genetics, international genetics) and steadier subscription/testing revenue (Farm software/MINDA, Herd testing). Government R&D tax incentive income (NZ$6.9m in FY2026) is booked within NZ revenue.

revenue_streams.name: NZ Market Genetics (AB straws, incl. sexed semen, insemination services)
revenue_streams.note: External revenue $131.1m FY2026 vs $119.9m FY2025 (+9.3%); sexed semen use up 52% YoY, genomic profiling up 19% YoY

revenue_streams.name: Testing (herd testing, DNA/animal health)
revenue_streams.note: External revenue $89.5m FY2026 vs $79.4m FY2025 (+12.7%); segment gross profit before tax jumped from $11.6m to $17.8m

revenue_streams.name: Farm software (MINDA SaaS, tags)
revenue_streams.note: External revenue $60.4m FY2026 vs $61.8m FY2025 (slightly down); recurring, over-time recognition; wearable-integration connected animals up 93.8% YoY signals platform stickiness

revenue_streams.name: International (offshore genetics)
revenue_streams.note: External revenue $17.4m FY2026 vs $16.0m FY2025; smallest and most volatile segment, includes LIC Ireland and Beacon Automation (Australia)

revenue_streams.name: Other (R&D, support services, inter-segment)
revenue_streams.note: Includes R&D tax incentive income and inter-segment eliminations

business_model.customer_type: B2B farmer-members and non-member NZ dairy farmers (co-operative pricing to shareholders); international genetics customers are offshore dairy breeders/AI companies
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~93% of revenue ($293.2m of $314.8m FY2026); Australia ~3%; Ireland ~1.4%; UK ~0.9%; Other ~1.7%
business_model.seasonality_note: LIC's Parent artificial-breeding business is highly seasonal: the majority of AB/genetics revenue is booked in H1 (spring mating, Oct-Dec) without a matching share of full-year costs. LIC's own H1-FY2026 filing states explicitly that 'November results...are not indicative of the second half result nor, therefore, the full year result.' H1 FY2026 underlying earnings were $36.8m against a full-year guided range of only $20-24m, implying H2 is loss-making at the underlying-earnings line most years. Any single half-year figure must be read in that context, not annualised.

main_competitors: World Wide Sires (US-based AB genetics exporter)
Independent/overseas semen importers and boutique NZ breeding companies
competitive_position.market_position: Historically dominant incumbent in NZ dairy AI/genetics and herd testing (long-run market share commonly cited in the 70-80% range for AB, though LIC does not disclose an exact figure in filings), facing entrenched, well-capitalised multinational competitors (CRV/Genus-ABS) that specifically market pasture-based genetics tailored to NZ systems.

moat_factors.description: ~100 years of NZ pasture-based dairy breeding data plus a genomic reference population exceeding two million genotypes; the LIC database is carried as an indefinite-life intangible asset ($10.5m) precisely because it is not readily replicable

MINDA herd-management software plus 17 third-party integration partners and wearable-device connectivity (animals connected up 93.8% YoY) create data lock-in and switching costs for farmers who have built years of herd records on the platform

moat_factors.factor: Scale/national footprint in testing and AB delivery
moat_factors.description: National herd-testing and insemination infrastructure is costly to replicate at LIC's scale across ~10,000 herds

Co-operative status and Dairy Industry Restructuring Act (DIRA)-linked shareholding rules (no person may hold >5% of ordinary shares) insulate LIC from takeover, but this is a governance shield, not a genuine competitive moat against rival genetics suppliers

weaknesses: Co-operative pricing mandate ('fair commercial prices' to shareholder-users) structurally caps margin expansion and the ability to extract economic value from the moat for outside (Investment Share) capital
Single-country revenue concentration (~93% NZ) tied to a shrinking/flat national dairy herd
Bull-team/genetics asset base is a depreciating, biologically-constrained resource requiring continuous reinvestment (R&D expense $26.6m FY2026, up from $22.5m)
History of costly offshore/technology missteps (Automation business divested June 2021; prior $20m+ 'transformation cost' episode in 2017-18) signals execution risk in strategic initiatives
International segment remains small and has not scaled into a meaningful profit contributor after years of investment

growth_drivers: Sexed semen adoption (+52% YoY in FY2026) shifting product mix toward higher-value genetics and improving herd replacement efficiency for farmers
Genomic profiling growth (+19% YoY; reference population now >2 million genotypes) deepening the core data moat and supporting premium genetics pricing
MINDA/wearable integration ecosystem expansion (connected animals +93.8% YoY, 17 integration partners, >two-thirds of farmers sharing data) as a platform for future data-monetisation and stickiness

Multi-year technology/enterprise-system replacement programme intended to modernise customer-facing systems and lower the cost-to-serve once complete (near-term cost, medium-term potential margin benefit)
Continued genetic-gain R&D (record $26.6m FY2026 R&D spend) targeting a 'lower-emitting, more efficient' herd of the future aligned with processor/export market requirements
Testing segment profitability improvement (segment gross profit before tax +53% YoY to $17.8m) suggests operating leverage as DNA/animal-health testing volumes grow

business.description: LIC has two share classes: farmer-held Co-operative Control Shares (voting, not NZX-traded) and NZX-quoted Investment/Ordinary Shares. Outside equity holders buying LIC.NZ hold Ordinary Shares that carry economic rights (dividends) but the company's constitution requires it to remain 'User Controlled' (eligible farmer-users must hold ≥60% of voting rights) and to sell core products/services to shareholders 'at fair commercial prices' rather than to maximise profit. The Constitution also caps any single holder at 5% of ordinary shares and effectively rules out a takeover (LIC states in its FY2026 report it 'considers it is not necessary to have takeover protocols in place'). No changes to this constitutional structure can occur without written Ministerial consent. Net effect: outside shareholders are minority economic participants in an entity legally structured to prioritise farmer-users, not shareholder returns — this is the dominant, structural reason FY2026 market capitalisation ($171.7m) sits well below net asset value ($304.4m), which LIC's own auditors flag as an impairment indicator (tested and cleared each year).

~93% of revenue and virtually all of the addressable market is the NZ dairy herd (~4.68m cows, ~10,000 herds per DairyNZ FY2024/25 stats), which has fallen ~12% over the past decade on land-use conversion (forestry, horticulture, urban) even as milksolids output has held up via productivity gains

business.risk: Milk-price cyclicality of farmer discretionary spend
business.description: Farmer willingness to pay for premium genetics/sexed semen/testing tracks the Fonterra Farmgate Milk Price; a weak payout compresses demand for LIC's higher-margin, more discretionary products

CRV Ambreed and ABS (Genus PLC) both actively market NZ pasture-specific genetics and have taken/contested market-share leadership claims historically; World Wide Sires and independent importers add further AB competition
LIC has previously exited underperforming offshore ventures (Automation business divested June 2021) and the current International segment remains small (~6% of revenue) with volatile profitability

financial.risk: Statutory earnings volatility from livestock/bull-team revaluation
financial.description: The bull team ($109.5m carrying value at FY2026) is fair-valued through profit or loss each period based on a Level 3 DCF model sensitive to Fonterra payout forecasts, WACC and bull run-off assumptions. FY2026 bull-team revaluation added $8.3m to pre-tax profit (FY2025: $12.3m; H1-FY2026: nil). This makes statutory NPAT a low-quality, non-cash-driven number; LIC itself strips it out (along with nil-paid-share fair-value movements and significant system-implementation costs) to report 'Underlying Earnings' as the basis for dividends.

The multi-year enterprise/customer-facing system replacement programme is expensed as incurred (SaaS-based, not capitalised): $9.0m pre-tax ($6.5m post-tax) in FY2026, following $3.0m ($2.0m post-tax) already incurred in H1-FY2026 alone. This is explicitly excluded from Underlying Earnings but does hit statutory NPAT (down 30.4% YoY to $21.3m in FY2026) and cash flow; total multi-year cost and end-date are not disclosed in the filings reviewed

regulatory.description: New Zealand's He Waka Eke Noa-derived farm-level emissions pricing framework remains a live, evolving policy area for the dairy sector; higher on-farm compliance costs could further pressure the milk-price-linked discretionary spend LIC depends on

National freshwater farm plan rollout has been paused pending simplification (with regional extensions, e.g. Southland to Nov-2027); an eventual stricter regime raises dairy farmers' compliance costs, an indirect drag on LIC's addressable spend

FMA confirmed 'no action' relief in Oct-2025 ahead of the Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill removing LIC's mandatory Climate Reporting Entity status — a modest compliance-cost tailwind, not a risk

macro.description: Fonterra's 2026/27 opening Farmgate Milk Price forecast of $9.75/kgMS (range $8.00-$11.00) was cut to $9.25/kgMS (range $8.00-$10.50) in July 2026 on an 11% GDT price fall and rising global supply — a direct read-through to FY2027 farmer spending power
Conversion of dairy land to forestry (carbon farming), horticulture and other uses structurally shrinks the addressable herd over time
LIC carries no bank debt at FY2026 year-end, limiting direct rate exposure, though farmer customers' own debt costs affect their spending capacity

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ dairy herd numbers have declined roughly 12% over the past decade (to ~4.68m cows per DairyNZ 2024/25 stats) while productivity gains have kept milksolids output broadly stable; industry commentary suggests herd numbers are stabilising into the 2025/26 season. The 2026/27 Fonterra Farmgate Milk Price was cut from an opening $9.75/kgMS to $9.25/kgMS (range $8.00-$10.50) in July 2026 on softening global demand and rising supply, a moderate headwind for FY2027 farmer discretionary spend on genetics/testing/software.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-high — LIC's higher-margin discretionary products (sexed semen, genomic profiling upgrades) track the milk-price cycle, while herd testing and MINDA subscriptions are stickier/more recurring
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct (debt-free balance sheet at FY2026 year-end; bank facilities in place to Feb-2027 for seasonal working capital only); indirect exposure via farmer customers' own borrowing costs
key_input_costs: People costs (largest opex line, $137.5m FY2026, +7.0% YoY)

recent_developments.event: FY2026 annual result (year ended 31 May 2026): revenue up 6.7% to $314.8m; statutory NPAT down 30.4% to $21.3m; underlying earnings flat at $21.8m (in line with the raised $20-24m guidance range); dividend of 12.26 cps declared ($17.5m, 80% of underlying earnings); total assets $408.5m, no debt

Fonterra cut the top end of its 2026/27 Farmgate Milk Price forecast to $9.25/kgMS (range $8.00-$10.50) from an opening $9.75/kgMS, citing an 11% fall in GDT reference prices and rising global milk supply

H1-FY2026 interim result (six months to 30 Nov 2025): revenue $195.2m (+5.2% YoY); statutory NPAT $33.8m (down from $39.1m, as the H1-FY2025 comparative had benefited from a $7.5m bull-team revaluation gain absent in H1-FY2026); underlying earnings $36.8m (up from $33.7m); management reaffirmed FY2026 underlying-earnings guidance of $20-24m; disclosed $4.0m pre-tax ($3.0m post-tax) of significant enterprise system implementation costs in H1 alone
Full-year guidance for FY2026 underlying earnings raised to $20-24m from the prior $18-22m range given at the FY2025 results
Annual Meeting: Nicola Shadbolt elected to the Board; Blair O'Keeffe appointed as Director (7 July 2025); Corrigan Sowman confirmed as Board Chair following a Chair transition

LIC continued to tidy legacy capital structure by fully paying up small remaining tranches of Nil Paid Shares (issued under a 2018 share simplification) into fully paid ordinary shares — an administrative clean-up, not a strategic capital restructure; 406,027 nil paid shares remained outstanding at FY2026 year-end alongside 142.3m quoted ordinary shares

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Result / H1-FY2026 Interim Result

items.notes: Guidance was raised from $18-22m (given at FY2025 results in mid-2025) to $20-24m (reaffirmed at H1-FY2026 in Jan-2026); actual $21.8m landed within the raised range and was flat versus FY2025's $21.7m (LIC restates FY2025 underlying earnings slightly to $21.746m for comparability)

FY2026 dividend of 12.26 cps ($17.5m) represented 80% of underlying earnings, consistent with the co-operative's historical dividend policy of returning the bulk of underlying earnings to shareholders while retaining capital for reinvestment

items.metric: No formal FY2027 quantitative guidance disclosed in filings reviewed
items.notes: LIC typically issues FY guidance at/after the H1 result (historically ~November/January) rather than at the FY annual report; no FY2027 underlying-earnings range had been published in the FY2026 annual report reviewed (dated 15 July 2026)

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CE David Chin) attributed the FY2026 NPAT decline 'predominately due to increased investment in upgrading technology and security platforms,' framing the multi-year enterprise-system replacement as necessary to protect growing volumes of farmer data and to keep MINDA/integration partnerships trustworthy and scalable. The Board characterised the co-operative as 'proud of the role we play in driving genetic gain' and pointed to sexed semen (+52%), genomic profiling (+19%) and wearable-integration growth (+93.8%) as evidence of demand strength, while offering no explicit view on the FY2026/27 milk-price downgrade's effect on FY2027 trading.

bull_case: Irreplicable ~100-year NZ pasture-genetics database plus a >2 million-genotype reference population gives LIC a durable technical edge that CRV Ambreed and ABS/Genus struggle to match for NZ-specific breeding outcomes
MINDA software and wearable-device integrations (connected animals +93.8% YoY, 17 partners) are building genuine data network effects and switching costs on top of the core genetics business
Debt-free balance sheet ($60.3m cash, no borrowings) with 80%-of-underlying-earnings dividend policy provides a defensible income stream once the current technology-investment cycle rolls off

Structural takeover-proof, farmer-aligned ownership (5% shareholding cap, co-operative constitution) removes activist/private-equity extraction risk that can destroy value at rival agri-input companies

Market cap ($171.7m) trades at a persistent, large discount to net assets ($304.4m) and to at least one third-party DCF estimate (~NZ$2.22/share cited by Simply Wall St vs ~NZ$1.09-1.21 recent trading), which some investors may view as a margin of safety if the co-op ever monetises assets or lifts payout
bear_case: Outside (Investment/Ordinary) shareholders have no realistic path to control or a takeover premium: the Constitution requires the company to remain 'User Controlled' (farmer-users ≥60% of votes), caps any holder at 5%, and can only be altered with Ministerial consent — the NAV discount is a structural feature, not a temporary mispricing, because LIC is legally obligated to price products to benefit farmer-shareholders rather than to maximise Ordinary Shareholder returns

Total addressable market (the NZ dairy herd) has shrunk ~12% over the past decade on land-use conversion and shows no clear sustained growth catalyst, capping the long-run top line regardless of execution

Statutory earnings are low-quality and volatile: bull-team fair-value revaluation added $8.3m to FY2026 pre-tax profit (swinging from +$12.3m in FY2025 to zero in H1-FY2026) and is directly geared to the Fonterra payout forecast, which was just cut for 2026/27

The multi-year technology/enterprise-system replacement programme is expensed (not capitalised), has already cost $9.0m pre-tax in FY2026 alone with no disclosed total budget or completion date, and drove a 30.4% fall in statutory NPAT — a real, ongoing cash and earnings drag with execution risk given LIC's history of costly prior 'transformation' initiatives

Farmer discretionary spend on LIC's higher-margin, more elastic products (sexed semen, genomic upgrades) is directly exposed to the Fonterra milk-price cycle, and the 2026/27 forecast was already trimmed from $9.75 to $9.25/kgMS on weak global dairy demand just as LIC heads into FY2027
